data.title: Bojná – a major Great Moravian centre in the Považský Inovec
data.excerpt: The hillfort of Bojná I – Valy was built on a rocky spur of the Považský Inovec at the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries and controlled the mountain routes between the Nitra region and the Váh region. Its almost 14-hectare enclosure, a rampart up to 10 m high on the outside, gilded plaques from a portable altar, a complete bell with its clapper and a hoard of 201 axe-shaped currency bars rank it among the key centres of the Principality of Nitra.
data.metaTitle: Bojná-Valy – a key Great Moravian centre on the Inovec
data.metaDescription: The hillfort of Bojná I–Valy in the Považský Inovec, from the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries: a key Great Moravian centre on the routes to the Váh.

keyFacts.label: Area of the Bojná I hillfort
keyFacts.value: Kidney-shaped plan, c. 600 m long, 200–300 m wide, total area of the acropolis with the bailey almost 14 ha

keyFacts.label: Fortification
keyFacts.value: Grillage-built rampart with a dry-stone facing, 3–5 m high from the inside and up to 10 m from the outside, base 18.5 m wide; two pincer-shaped gateways serving as a kind of toll station

keyFacts.label: Plaques and the small altar
keyFacts.value: 6 gilded plaques (circular and cross-shaped, depicting angelic/Christ figures) plus 3 frames, part of a portable altar with links to the Adriatic region

keyFacts.label: The Bojná bell
keyFacts.value: Height 160 mm, diameter 192 mm, weight 2,180 g — parallels in Italy (Canino, the Vatican) and Germany (Verden, Oldenburg), dated to the turn of the 8th/9th and the early 9th century

keyFacts.label: Military finds
keyFacts.value: Axe-shaped currency bars (201 in a single hoard), fragments of mail armour, a spur damascened with gold, the end mount of a sword scabbard with falcons, the stolen helmet of a Slavic warrior

keyFacts.label: The settlement complex
keyFacts.value: An agglomeration of four hillforts (Bojná I – Valy, II, III, IV), of which II and III had a supplementary guard function in controlling the road across the Považský Inovec

keyFacts.label: Duration of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: Total existence estimated at 120 years, with two destruction horizons (the beginning of the 9th century and after 906)

timeline.title: A refuge at Bojná II
timeline.description: At the time of the Marcomannic Wars the hilltop settlement of Hradisko (Bojná II) served as a place of refuge; denarii of Marcus Aurelius and a hoard of 15 coins with the latest issue of Valentinian I were found.

timeline.title: Occupation in the Migration Period
timeline.description: A bronze bow brooch dates the end of this phase of occupation at Bojná II; finds of Roman/federate military belts attest contacts with the frontier zone.

timeline.title: A portable altar with plaques
timeline.description: A set of 6 gilded plaques and 3 frames, probably part of an altare portabile with a central (unpreserved) seventh plaque depicting Christ.

timeline.title: A synod on the banks of the Danube
timeline.description: A Frankish synod prepared a programme for the Christianisation of the area of the Avars defeated by the Franks, which opened the way for Bavarian and Aquileian missionaries into the Nitra region as well.

timeline.title: The hillfort of Bojná I – Valy is built
timeline.description: Built as part of an extensive agglomeration (Bojná I, II, III, IV); kidney-shaped plan, a rampart 3–10 m high, two pincer-shaped gateways on the longitudinal axis.

timeline.title: First flourishing and first destruction
timeline.description: Bojná reached its greatest flourishing and at the same time was destroyed for the first time by fire — both building phases of the rampart were destroyed by fire.

timeline.title: New fortification works
timeline.description: A beam from the edge of a rampart chamber dated by dendrochronology — the year of King Svatopluk's death and of Svatopluk II's accession; the old beams were replaced by new ones.

timeline.title: The second destruction of the hillfort
timeline.description: Probably attacks by Old Hungarian armies, possibly in cooperation with local commanders — besides Hungarian arrows, a large number of non-Hungarian ones occurs in the destruction layer.

timeline.title: The central part of the hillfort uncovered
timeline.description: Sunken and ground-level dwellings with stone and clay ovens, production workshops and a large building with a stone footing.

timeline.title: A new interpretation by Karol Pieta
timeline.description: Vedecká cukráreň science café (27 October 2009) — Bojná described as an extensive agglomeration comprising Bojná I, II, III and IV, compared to Mikulčice and Pompeii.

timeline.title: Funded research continues
timeline.description: The Slovak Academy of Sciences and the Research and Development Agency allocated funds for fieldwork at Bojná and at other sites (Bíňa, Pobedim, Majcichov).

timeline.title: A planned archaeological open-air museum
timeline.description: The Institute of Archaeology SAS and the village of Bojná announced their intention to build a replica of a Slavic house and later a whole archaeological park near Ranč pod Babicou.

children.text: BOJNÁ I – Valy

Bojná I – Valy, as this early medieval site is actually called, probably came into being at the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries, or in the first decades of the 9th century. It lies in the Považský Inovec range, on a rocky spur of the main massif at an elevation of 390–430 m above sea level. In the Middle Hillfort period this range was threaded with many routes, which offered the most convenient link between the Nitra region and the Váh region. The importance of these crossings is underlined by the great number of sites of that period on both sides of the Považský Inovec. On the Nitra side these are, besides Bojná I, also Bojná II and III, Marhát, Úhrad and Nitrianska Blatnica – Jurko. On the Váh side lie Pobedim, Ducové and Hrádok. All the sites can easily be reached from one another within a short span of time.

blocks.caption: Bojná. Photo: Naj
blocks.alt: Bojná. Photo: Naj

children.text: When to the facts mentioned above we add the dense occupation not only on the acropolis and in the bailey but also outside the defences, together with the interesting finds that will be discussed below, and the results of mining archaeology, which has discovered worked-out iron-ore deposits, various quarries and extraction pits, it is entirely justified to rank Bojná I among the important sites not only within the Principality of Nitra but within the whole Great Moravian empire. As the most recent interpretations by archaeologists state (PhDr. Karol Pieta, DrSc., Vedecká cukráreň science café, 27 October 2009), on the basis of the latest excavations Bojná can be described as an extensive agglomeration comprising not only the hillfort of Bojná I but also Bojná II, III and, most recently, Bojná IV, which Karol Pieta mentions in the discussion referred to. In a sense Bojná could be compared to Mikulčice, in that its demise came about in a similarly sudden way, but above all because — unlike many other sites in Slovakia, where medieval towns later grew up on the foundations of a hillfort and thus gradually destroyed the original buildings and precious artefacts — Bojná was one of the few sites where permanent occupation did not continue after its demise, and the destroyed hillfort gradually sank into oblivion together with all the wealth that lay there at the moment of its sudden end. For this reason Bojná, like Mikulčice, Pompeii and the like, is a marvellous source of knowledge for archaeology today. It is only a pity that, before the archaeologists came to their senses, Bojná had been discovered by various treasure hunters, who undoubtedly caused great damage by seizing the most interesting finds. On the other hand, it must be said that the famous gilded plaques, for instance, were found by just such a hunter, who handed them over.

The hillfort is kidney-shaped; its longitudinal axis is about 600 m long and its transverse axes measure from 200 to 300 metres. The total area of the acropolis together with the bailey reaches almost 14 ha. A very well preserved rampart winds around the whole enclosure, reaching a height of 3–5 m on the inner side and up to 10 m on the outer, while its base is about 18.5 m wide. The main
rampart was built with a grillage construction and faced on the outside with a dry-stone revetment.
In front of the rampart lies an outer
ditch

, and this form of fortification is repeated once more, on a smaller scale, around the hillfort, while to the west there is yet another rampart. On the whole, far more time was devoted to the defences on the western side, and the other hillforts in the Nitra part also have strengthened fortifications in their western sections. It is clear that the inhabitants of the Nitra region expected an attack from the direction of the Váh; the Moravian principality comes into consideration as a potential enemy, but it could equally have been another important Slavic tribe from the Váh region, for example the one seated at Divinka near Žilina. The main line of the rampart is broken by two gateways facing each other, placed on the longitudinal axis of the hillfort. Both are pincer-shaped, that is, they are turned inwards into the enclosure. A road led through the hillfort by way of these gateways. Prague Castle was arranged in a similar way in its beginnings. The unusual placing of the gateways on the longitudinal axis of the hillfort, and at the same time on the road from the Nitra region to the Váh region, suggests that Bojná probably served, among other things, as a kind of toll station — anyone (above all merchants) who wished to pass through this important mountain crossing could not avoid Bojná, but had to stop here and pay, and at the same time had the opportunity to offer his own goods or to buy others.

children.text: According to the report on the excavation of the hillfort
of 2008, in the central part of the inner enclosure of the hillfort there were uncovered
sunken and ground-level dwellings with stone and clay ovens and production workshops, as well as a large building with a stone footing
. According to the results of test trenching, the
bailey was protected by a wide ditch cut into the rock bedrock and by a rampart with an internal grillage construction and a stone facing at the front.
The large
circuit rampart
was sectioned in the eastern part of the hillfort, where its profile stood 530 cm high above the bedrock.
Its core was interleaved with timber grillages held on both sides by rows of posts linked with wattle

. The front part above the outer ditch was built in log technique. On the inner side of the construction there were log chambers. Hoards were found in several of them. Both building phases of the rampart were destroyed by fire. During the excavation a large quantity of pottery and 800 inventory numbers of artefacts were recovered. The important finds include the clapper of another bell, gilded bronze mounts, numerous spurs and several fragments of mail armour.

blocks.caption: A view of the hillfort from the east (Naj)
blocks.alt: A view of the hillfort from the east (Naj)

children.text: In 2008, sunken and ground-level dwellings with stone or clay ovens were uncovered in the central part of the hillfort. Production workshops and a large building with a stone footing were found as well.
The hillfort has
two periods of demise
. The first of them belongs to the period of
Pribina's principality,

that is, the beginning of the 9th century. In this period Bojná probably reached its greatest flourishing and at the same time was destroyed for the first time. The second time, the hillfort was laid waste at the beginning of the 10th century,
probably
by attacks of Old Hungarian armies.

More precise dating was obtained by means of dendrochronology: according to Karol Pieta, one of the beams that formed the edge of a chamber of the rampart was dated by dendrochronology to the year 894 — that is, to the year in which King Svatopluk died and his son Svatopluk II ascended the Great Moravian throne. It is therefore clear that in 894 new fortification works were carried out at Bojná, when the old beams, which by then were several decades old and may be assumed not to have been in good condition, were presumably replaced by new ones, thereby improving the hillfort's defensive capability. When exactly the second destruction of the hillfort took place is not yet known; it can only be supposed that it may have been after the battle of Bratislava in 906. Since the destruction layer contains, besides Old Hungarian arrows, also a large number of non-Hungarian ones, this may lead to the assumption that already at this time the Hungarian armies were cooperating with some local commanders, or local forces. This may be a reflection of the internal instability of Great Moravia after the death of a strong ruler, when some magnates evidently had no interest in the continued existence of central power and even joined forces with marauding raiders in order to break it up. The total duration of the hillfort has so far been set at 120 years.

blocks.alt: A view of Bojná and its surroundings from Marhát hill (Naj)

children.text: Finds
5 hoards, the set of plaques, the bell and a large number of smaller finds come from the site of Bojná – Valy I. A large part of them belongs to the Blatnica–Mikulčice horizon.
The plaques

6 plaques of gilded copper in varying states of preservation were found, together with a few unassigned fragments, probably from these plaques. In addition there are 3 strip-like frames, likewise of gilded copper, joined into a circle from a single piece of sheet metal or from 2 or more parts. Two of them are complete, the third survives as a fragment. The attempt to reconstruct the arrangement of the plaques and frames proceeded from their number and from the mutual relationship of the individual artefacts, with emphasis on symmetry and on the hierarchy of meaning.

The plaques are of two shapes and sizes. 4 circular ones with a diameter of 150 mm were found, while 2 have the shape of an equal-armed cross and a diameter of 133 mm. Circular plaques 1, 2 and 3 are bordered by a frame decorated with alternating empty triangles and triangles filled with punched dots; plaque 4 differs from them in having a border in the form of a line of semicircular arcs. The edges of the cross-shaped plaques end in double bands of beaded punching.

blocks.caption: Excavation of the rampart
blocks.alt: Excavation of the rampart

children.text: One of the important questions is the function of the three circular frames, of which two complete examples were handed over together with the plaques, while the incomplete third example, consisting of three fragments, was found during a re-examination at the place of the earlier find. One possibility is that complete circles of the same type could have formed the border of both cross-shaped plaques. This, however, is not certain. They could also have framed other images which have not survived, and these could even have been of organic material, for example textile. According to this reconstruction, the original set could have consisted of seven plaques.

A substantial part of frame 3 was found during the excavation directly at the find spot, probably still in the in situ position of the whole set. Which combination applies remains a matter for further consideration: whether this third frame was used in the same way as the other two — to frame further plaques — or whether it emphasised the importance of one of the circular plaques as its second, outer frame. That is why it differs in part from the two complete frames; it could also have belonged to a further, possibly central, seventh plaque, which was not in the hoard or did not survive. Karol Pieta and Alexander Ruttkay incline to the thesis of 7 plaques, 3 of which were encircled by circular frames. The seventh plaque should have been the central one and should have depicted Christ. The set was probably part of a portable altar, an altare portabile. Such caskets held either liturgical objects or the relics of saints. Occasionally a casket contained both together. These portable altars were usually decorated with scenes from the gospels and with angels or other sacred beings. Specialists estimate its size at a minimum of 300 × 600 × 300 (mm). A very interesting discovery is the letters on two of the plaques discussed below. They belong to the sphere of Latin Western Christianity, yet a Greek influence can be observed in the letters.

blocks.caption: A photograph from June 2013 by V. Satko - the second Slavic log house is almost finished
blocks.alt: A photograph from June 2013 by V. Satko - the second Slavic log house is almost finished

children.text: The dating of the plaques is indirect and rests on the dating of the other finds from Bojná I, which belong to the beginning of the first half of the 9th century. A group of German researchers who undertook to reconstruct the portable altar settled on a date between AD 780 and 820.
The plaques are circular and cross-shaped. The circular ones probably formed a kind of border for the cross-shaped ones.
Circular plaques
Plaque 1

blocks.caption: The helmet, probably of a Slavic warrior, from Bojná and part of the mail aventail from the helmet. This European rarity was stolen from the hillfort by a metal detectorist and subsequently sold at auction. Slovakia thus lost an exceptionally valuable artefact of the early Slavic past. For information leading to the tracing of the helmet we offer a reward of several hundred euros. (photograph from the book by K. Pieta et al.: Bojná 2)
blocks.alt: The helmet, probably of a Slavic warrior, from Bojná and part of the mail aventail from the helmet — stolen from the hillfort by a metal detectorist and sold at auction.

children.text: This plaque bears the figure of a man with his head en face, with a shape resembling a Maltese cross in the background. The figure has its left arm raised at a right angle. From below the elbow what is probably feathering protrudes. On the right side the arm is missing, but the whole wing can be seen. The figure is dressed in a tunic. Beneath the left arm are the Latin letters SVAVM. This is probably Christ with wings, the so-called Christus-Engel. This type of figure arose, it seems, by the reduction of angels that originally stood at its sides.
Plaque 2

It shows a standing male figure with raised arms. In the left hand it holds an object in the shape of the letter T with a widened base. Behind the arms we can again notice groups of three feathers representing wings. This person could be St Anthony the Hermit, since the object in the shape of a T may be an Antonine cross combined with a little bell, which are the attributes of this saint. It is St Anthony who stands at the beginning of the Christian pilgrimage traditions and of the rise of monastic communities.
Plaque 3

This considerably damaged plaque has in its central part a symmetrically placed figure of a man, again in the en face position. His hands are folded on his chest and above his shoulders are outspread wings. At the figure's left side are the Latin letters ...NDE
Plaque 4

The most badly damaged plaque. It differs from the other circular plaques in that the border is not filled with triangles but with small arcs. The figure is en face, the hands raised in a gesture of adoration. The wings are folded beneath the arms.

children.text: Cross-shaped plaques
Plaque 5

A plaque preserved practically complete. In the centre a male figure is depicted with his head slightly raised, from which rounded hair, or flames, rise on both sides. On the chest the figure either has hands joined in prayer, or this is a plastron, that is, a double breastplate. Outspread wings issue directly from the shoulders.
Plaque 6

It shows an upright figure. It has two pairs of wings, one pair folded on the chest and the other at the right side of the trunk. The arms are spread with an upward tendency. The set is completed by 3 frames 19–20 mm wide and 190–192 mm in diameter. The decoration consists of alternating triangles, just as on the circular plaques.
Bells

The bell was discovered in the north-eastern part of the hillfort. It survives as a single whole, if we do not count the iron clapper, which was found in the immediate vicinity of the bell. The height of the bell is 160 mm, the outer diameter of the sound bow is 192 mm and the wall thickness is from 2 to 6 mm. Its weight is 2,180 g. The clapper is 170 mm long and weighs 200 g. The bell alloy contains a predominant proportion of copper supplemented by tin, lead, iron and silver.

blocks.alt: One possible visualisation of the small altar (K. Pieta)

children.text: A further 2 fragments of a bell's body and a second clapper were found within the hillfort enclosure. Metallographic analyses established that the fragments come from 3 different bells. Suitable parallels to the surviving bell are to be found above all in Italy (Canino, the Vatican) and Germany (Verden, Oldenburg — the clapper of the surviving Bojná bell is typologically identical with the clapper of the latter bell). The Italian bells are dated to the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries and the German ones to the beginning of the 9th century. The question why 2 bells were completely smashed may be connected with possible religious conflicts between the old pagan religion and the incoming Christianity. The bells could have been symbolically destroyed in the course of such a conflict. The possibility of some kind of pagan uprising could also be one of the causes of the first destruction of the hillfort in the time of Pribina — whether the hillfort was destroyed by Mojmír's armies we cannot yet say with certainty.

blocks.alt: Bojná – a major Great Moravian centre

children.text: A short film from the workshop of Mr Dvořák – The bell of Bojná:

Since there are sacred buildings in the surroundings of Bojná (the rotundas at Ducové and Nitrianska Blatnica are proportionally very similar to church 6 at Mikulčice) whose origin lies in the Adriatic region, a missionary route from precisely this area is being considered. This supposition may be confirmed by the fact that in 796 a synod was held directly in the interior of the territory of the Avars defeated by the Franks, somewhere “on the banks of the Danube”, and its aim was to prepare a programme for the Christianisation of that area, which opened the way into the Nitra region as well, chiefly for Bavarian and Aquileian missionaries.
Further finds

Among the other finds, a gilded bronze strap end made in the chip-carving technique certainly deserves mention. What is certainly of interest is that an almost identical strap end was found in the grave goods of a man at Modrá near Velehrad. It is important to realise that, apart from this case, we know of no two even similar artefacts of this type with chip-carved decoration from the Early Middle Ages. It is therefore possible that both strap ends come from a single workshop, or even from a single master craftsman.

blocks.alt: Bojná – a major Great Moravian centre

children.text: The most numerous are structural elements such as cramps, nails and hooks. Further, 201 axe-shaped currency bars were found here in a single hoard, and roughly the same number in the immediate surroundings of the hillfort. There is likewise a large number of knives, axes, chisels, small saws, drawknives, spoon augers, iron fittings of buckets and one chain made up of 21 links; these objects point to a fairly developed craft production. The iron mining and processing mentioned above, as well as other metallurgical activity, is confirmed by a quantity of slag, bronze casting lumps, smithing waste and specialised tools for this work.

Agriculture is attested by 2 types of sickle (an elongated curved type and a type with a short knife-like blade), goads, coulters, hoes, ploughshares and cutting blades. Among the military items, rhomboid arrowheads with a tang were found, and, in smaller numbers, arrows with barbs and a long socket, axes, cruciform mounts and the ferrule of a spear. The Slavs, however, probably did not protect the butts of their spears in this way, so this may be an import. From horse harness, bits, stirrups and spurs were found. One of the spurs is damascened with gold. The most recent discovery is several fragments of mail armour. A large number of metal costume fittings was also found, such as the strap end already mentioned, or mounts and buckles. Many are gilded or damascened with silver. Two bronze weights are probably evidence of trade.

blocks.alt: Bojná – a major Great Moravian centre

children.text: Systematic excavation is under way at the site of Bojná I – Valy; these are not merely random trenches. The aims of the excavation were summed up by its director, Karol Pieta of the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra. “Where there is a mission, there is also a church. But it could have been of wood, and in that case it need not have survived.” He assumes that besides this they will find houses, production workshops, cemeteries and perhaps even buildings of palatial type. Pieta stressed that the fortification is extraordinarily large, which will make the excavation demanding both technically and financially.
I am adding current information about the further excavation planned at Bojná (from the website www.obnova.sk):

“Archaeological excavation at Bojná in the Topoľčany district will continue in the coming years as well. The Slovak Academy of Sciences has earmarked funds in its budget for fieldwork this year. For 2012, 2013 and 2014 the archaeologists succeeded in obtaining money under a project approved by the Research and Development Agency. The grant is at the same time intended for excavations at other important early medieval sites such as Bíňa, Pobedim and Majcichov.

blocks.alt: Bojná – a major Great Moravian centre

children.text: Excavation at Bojná usually begins in June and lasts until late autumn. “This year we plan to complete the investigation of the hillfort's large fortification, which is very important for the precise dating of the site and for an understanding of the building techniques of the ninth and early tenth centuries,” the director of the excavation, Karol Pieta of the Institute of Archaeology SAS in Nitra, told the SITA news agency. The archaeologists will also turn their attention to the Slavic burial mounds, five of which have been found here so far. For the time being they have examined only the largest of them, 15 metres in diameter. “Unfortunately, it is apparently only a symbolic grave and, what is more, it had been robbed. It is, however, very interesting from the point of view of burial rituals,” Pieta said. In the mound were found the remains of a funeral pyre and of a funeral feast, animal bones and weapons. A warrior who had fallen away from Bojná was probably buried here symbolically.

blocks.alt: Bojná – a major Great Moravian centre

children.text: The most interesting find of last year was the end mount of a sword scabbard, richly decorated with silver. Falcons taking flight are depicted on it. “It is a find for which it has not yet been possible to find any parallel, and it safely demonstrates the presence of the highest social stratum of the time,” Pieta pointed out. In the last excavation season the archaeologists also managed to clarify the layout of the settlement that lay inside the hillfort. In its centre two large features were found, of which the footings of the foundations survive. By their size and by the finds in their vicinity they can unambiguously be linked with the presence of the social elite, Pieta stated. The settlement consisted of manorial courts made up of sunken-featured buildings and ground-level farm buildings. The sunken-featured buildings are typical Slavic dwellings with a stone oven, cut into the underlying rock. In future the scholars want to present the best-preserved features to the public.”
BOJNÁ II

blocks.alt: Bojná – a major Great Moravian centre

children.text: In the immediate vicinity of the Valy hillfort there are 2 further hillforts, designated Bojná II and Bojná III. On the hillfort of Bojná II, Pieta states among other things:

“The elevation known as „Hradisko“ (335 m above sea level) in the northern part of the cadastral area of the village of Bojná, Topoľčany district, controls the narrows of the valley of the little river Bojnianka, along which an old road, today hardly used, ran between the Váh region and the Nitra region across the Považský Inovec range. Material obtained by test trenching confirmed occupation from the end of the Early Roman period, from the Migration Period and from the Early Middle Ages, probably from the beginning of the 9th century. A complex system of fortification is relatively clearly visible in the terrain, supplementing the natural protection of this place — steep precipices on the western and southern sides and a deep gully on the north-east of the site (Fig. 2). The rampart bank running around the perimeter of the plateau is highest opposite the easily accessible neck of land to the north. The fortification is pronounced in this part, formed by a line of a doubled system of rampart and ditch. Here, too, is the entrance into the enclosure, passing perpendicular to the defences. Its present width (we do not know whether original or recently widened) is about 3 m. Towards the west the fortification continues for only 25–30 m and is joined by a line which ends above the steep slope of the hill. The outer rampart at this point reaches a height of 3–3.5 m. Further from the entrance — towards the east — the line of the circuit defences descends gently along with the slope and turns to the south-east. From this circuit fortification another rampart, about 85 m long, runs out perpendicularly to the north, with a ditch on its western side. In this way a fortified bailey was created. At the point where the two ramparts meet, a slight rise is visible in the terrain, which suggests the existence of a tower.

blocks.alt: Bojná – a major Great Moravian centre

children.text: Besides pottery, several stray coins, a brooch and the attachment of a bronze jug were found at Hradisko. Two denarii of Marcus Aurelius and further objects belong unambiguously to the second half of the 2nd century. In this period, when Germanic peoples lived in the territory of present-day Slovakia, and which corresponds roughly to the time of the so-called Marcomannic Wars, a whole series of hilltop settlements, probably places of refuge, appears in the northern part of the Carpathian Basin — both in the area of Suebic occupation in western and central Slovakia and on the old, disused hillforts of the declining Púchov culture in the north of the territory of present-day Slovakia (Pieta 1994). We assume that Hradisko, like many other sites, served in the troubled times of the second half of the 2nd century as a hilltop settlement — a refuge for the protection of local communities from the densely populated Váh region around Pobedim or from an as yet unidentified settlement zone in the adjacent part of the Nitra river basin. At Bojná II, finds from the Migration Period are the most strongly represented. They were scattered inside, but also outside, the fortified area.

blocks.alt: Bojná – a major Great Moravian centre

children.text: A valuable coin hoard was also found at the hillfort, consisting of fifteen worn bronze coins, the latest issue being that of Valentinian I. Such hoards are characteristic of the earlier phase of the Migration Period in the northern part of the Middle Danube region, where old coins evidently replaced the missing currency. An interesting new element in this milieu are fragments of metal components of Roman or federate military belts — buckles with animal heads and decorative mounts. They are evidence of the contacts of this peripheral submontane area with the provinces and chiefly with the frontier zone in the final stage of Roman administration. For determining the end of the occupation, a bronze bow brooch with three knobs on a semicircular head plate is significant; it can reliably be dated to the second half of the 5th century. Some finds show traces of the presence of a higher social stratum. Hilltop settlements are a characteristic phenomenon of the beginning of the Migration Period, both in the Danubian area with its Late Suebic occupation and in northern Slovakia with the occupation of the North Carpathian group. Only recently have sites appeared which evidently also existed around the middle of the 5th century. According to stray finds, some of them were used at the end of the 5th and the beginning of the 6th century as well. A good example is the settlement of Bojná II presented here. The Slavic finds so far from the Bojná II site are not numerous, yet to a lesser degree they are nevertheless represented. The fortification at Bojná II, with its pronounced double rampart on the northern side, has not yet been dated. We may assume, however, that it must have been built, or else renewed or rebuilt, in the Early Middle Ages, when the site chiefly fulfilled a military and guard function. The system of doubled belts of ditches with ramparts is repeated in the case of both of the other, evidently early medieval, fortifications at Bojná.”

children.text: Photographs of the Bojná II hillfort (by Ľubomír Červený):
BOJNÁ III.
K. Pieta summed up his insights on the third hillfort as follows:

“Between the Hradská valley with the hillfort of Bojná I and the valley of the Bojnianka lies a low mountain ridge which forms part of a more extensive massif, the Zihľavník. At the point where it narrows on both sides, an earthen fortification was built which is relatively indistinct in the terrain and forms a complex system of ditches and ramparts. To the north, the south and the east the banks with ditches are visible only in places and their full course has not yet been reliably established and surveyed. On the western side (as in the case of Bojná I) the enclosure was fortified by a double line of ditches and ramparts, with two passages through both fortification belts. Today's forest road crosses the middle of the rise transversely through the ramparts by way of a passage which was evidently made in modern times. The mountain ridge is still used today as a convenient forest road without great differences in height. It is therefore probable that this route was used in the past as well (perhaps chiefly in the winter months, when the valleys were difficult to pass). Fortification III, like Bojná I and II, came into being in order to control several lines of the same long-distance route. The fortification has not yet been investigated and for dating we have at our disposal only the not very numerous finds from the interior of the hillfort. These are for the most part early medieval pottery and iron objects without the possibility of closer dating. Roughly in the middle of the enclosure, test trenching examined a pit with diagnostic pottery of approximately the 8th–9th centuries. Among the iron objects, small knives, nails, structural fittings and fragments of keys predominate. Traces of production are absent. Weapons are represented by a small axe, arrowheads with barbs and a small fragment of a mail shirt with large riveted links. Only a relatively small number of finds was obtained at the site. Their composition emphasises the military rather than the settlement character of the site. The structure was probably put up in haste and was used only for a short time. Hillforts I and III had a through-route character. They were built on roughly the same kind of terrain — on a mountain ridge, in a position which in earlier periods was not sought out for defensive purposes. It seems that in the case of both these hillforts the common motive for their construction was control of the road which passed through them. This is a remarkable phenomenon, which certainly deserves greater attention in a more detailed assessment of the whole settlement area. Compared with the large hillfort I, with its truly extraordinary fortification, both of the small early medieval fortifications of Bojná II and III fulfilled, according to the present state of research, only secondary but undoubtedly important tasks in the defence of the wider area of this part of the eastern foothills of the Považský Inovec, and strategically supported the security of the hinterland of the central hillfort. They were probably not occupied for any length of time. The direction of a potential attack from the Váh side across the range is clear from the doubled defences both at Valy and on Žihľavník. In this respect, the need to secure the Nitra region against the historically attested attack from the Moravian side (the conflict between Mojmír and Pribina) suggests itself as an explanation.

Will there be an archaeological open-air museum at Bojná?
I am adding a very interesting press release:
(06.08.2011; www.aktuality.sk; Regióny, 15.15, p.; TASR)

In future, visitors to the village or to the site itself will also be able to touch the results of the archaeological excavations at the magnate's hillfort of Bojná with their own hands. Together with the municipal office, the archaeologists want to build replicas of Slavic dwellings here, and an archaeological open-air museum in which they will construct part of a Great Moravian settlement using the methods of experimental archaeology.

“We want to prepare some of the already excavated areas with very attractive original structures for opening to the public. We also want to reconstruct one of the Slavic houses. It should be an ordinary standard Slavic house, a sunken-featured building.

They were small houses, roughly three by three metres in plan, consisting of a large stone hearth and a sleeping place. People spent most of their time outdoors, where ordinary domestic work was also carried out, and in the huts they only cooked and slept,” explained the director of the archaeological excavation at the Bojná hillfort, Karol Pieta. As he stated, the scholars were fortunate in that the foundations of several houses remained well preserved even after more than a thousand years, together with the furnishings that had once been in them.

“That means that by the oven we found vessels standing, in one corner an axe was propped up, in another corner there was horse harness and so on. So we have a whole series of such interesting details. We found the hoops of a wooden barrel, so we know that it stood there, even though we shall no longer discover whether it held beer, water or mead,” Pieta said. In the first phase the archaeologists want to build a reconstruction of a typical Slavic hut. It will stand directly within the hillfort enclosure. “That little house will be open and accessible.

It will be made in such a way that if someone even spends the night there, the world will not collapse. That is why we shall not install any more valuable objects there,” he explained. Building the archaeological open-air museum is, in his words, a considerably more complicated undertaking. It should stand near Ranč pod Babicou, and according to its mayor, Jozef Vanč, the village is already looking for a suitable plot of land.

Building the open-air museum already requires a building permit and sufficient funds. The Institute of Archaeology SAS in Nitra and the village of Bojná want to obtain these from European funds. “An archaeological park already requires infrastructure, an information centre and a certain amount of coordination. We would like to have at least the rough outlines of this project ready by the autumn.

In such parks or open-air museums what is usually presented is, let us say, a whole settlement, where there would be not only dwelling houses but also workshops, farm buildings, a church and graves. Quite simply everything, so that people have an all-round idea of how life at Bojná was lived. Where the well-known Bojná bell would hang in a bell cote and where the finds made at Bojná would also be presented directly. Whether agricultural tools, craft tools, ploughs, scythes and all those objects that the Slavs needed in everyday life,” Pieta said. Let us keep our fingers crossed that at last a full-fledged archaeological open-air museum of the Great Moravian period will come into being in Slovakia as well.
